You are working in a git worktree of the JusPrin repository (an OrcaSlicer fork, C++17, wxWidgets, CMake). Confirm first with `git log --oneline -1` that HEAD is commit eff2bdb6af "Define the token contract for the style sweep". If it is not, stop and report. Run every command with absolute paths inside your worktree; never touch /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin (the main checkout) or any other worktree. Commit on your branch when done and do not push.

Read agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md and agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md before editing. You must not change any OrcaSlicer-owned file. Everything you touch is under src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/ and tests/. Do not edit resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json; another agent owns it. Do not edit files under src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/; another agent owns those.

## Context

`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/ShellTheme.{hpp,cpp}` loads resources/jusprin/ui/design-tokens.json and exposes `palette(bool dark)` returning a `ShellPalette` of wxColours. It parses colour only. Fork-owned shell widgets (HeaderControls, StatusRow, SpoolMenu, SliceReviewPanel, AgentPane, McpConnectionDialog, Agent/AgentWebView) receive `const ShellTheme&` by constructor and read the palette, but they pick fonts by hand from OrcaSlicer's `Label::Body_12` / `Label::Head_14` presets (26 sites, 16 in HeaderControls, some using combinations the design system does not define such as bold 14 and regular 12) and write radii and component sizes as `FromDIP(4)`, `FromDIP(wxSize(28,34))`, and so on.

The theme is loaded twice: `Brand/BrandPalette.cpp` keeps a static instance for the OrcaSlicer colour overrides, and `Shell/ShellController.cpp` loads its own member copy.

The token JSON now carries (read it): `dimension.radius` {standard, compact, container, window, pill}, `dimension.space`, `typography.roles` {pageTitle, section, body, label, metadata} each with size, lineHeight, weight, `typography.technical`, and `component` entries: button recipes (compact, window, choice, parameter, icon, expanded, each with a textRole), chip {height 28, radius 4}, menuRow {height 36, radius 0}, popover {paddingY 8, rowGap 2, radius 8}, statusRow {height 34}, swatch {size 24, radius 4}. All numbers are DIP; callers wrap them in `FromDIP()`.

## Task

1. Extend ShellTheme, keeping the existing colour API unchanged:
   - Add a `ShellMetrics` struct parsed from `dimension` and `component`: the four named radii plus pill, the spacing steps, and one nested struct per component entry (chip, menu_row, popover, status_row, swatch, and the six button recipes with their sizes, padding, radius, and text role). Expose `const ShellMetrics& metrics() const`. Parsing failures throw `std::runtime_error` like the colour parser does.
   - Add `enum class TextRole { PageTitle, Section, Body, Label, Metadata, Technical }` and `const wxFont& font(TextRole) const`. Build each font once from the JSON role through OrcaSlicer's public `Label::sysFont(int size, bool bold)` (see src/slic3r/GUI/Widgets/Label.hpp; bold when weight is 700). Technical uses the body size with `wxFontInfo(...).Family(wxFONTFAMILY_TELETYPE)`, the way `technical_font()` in HeaderControls.cpp does today. Do not add any role the JSON does not have.
   - Load once: give `Brand/BrandPalette.hpp` a public `const ShellTheme* brand_theme()` returning the instance it already keeps (nullptr when the file failed to load), and make ShellController use it instead of calling `load_from_resources()` itself. ShellController currently treats a load failure as "leave the stock presentation untouched" by letting the exception propagate; preserve that behaviour by throwing the same `std::runtime_error` when `brand_theme()` is null.

2. Migrate `Shell/HeaderControls.cpp` and `.hpp` only (the other widgets are a later task). Replace every `Label::…` font choice with `m_theme.font(TextRole::…)`, every radius literal with `metrics()` values, the chip height 28 and the 34 with the chip and status-row entries, popover padding and row gap with the popover entry, and delete the local `technical_font()`. Where the current code uses a combination the roles do not define (bold 14, regular 12), pick the nearest role, keep a one-line comment saying what it was, and list each such decision in your report. Spacing such as `FromDIP(8)` for gaps may stay literal if the value is on the scale.

3. Add tests. tests/jusprin/ has a GUI-free Catch2 target (`jusprin_tests`, see its CMakeLists.txt); tests/shell/ has a wx-linked harness. Add a test that parses the real token file through ShellTheme and checks `metrics().radius_standard == 4`, `metrics().chip.height == 28`, and that `font(TextRole::Label)` is bold and `font(TextRole::Body)` is not. If ShellTheme cannot be linked into `jusprin_tests` without wx, put the test where it can link and say so.

4. Build. Configure a build directory inside your worktree with:
```
cmake -B <worktree>/build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON
```
Then build the `libslic3r_gui` target and your test target with `cmake --build <absolute build dir> --config RelWithDebInfo --target <targets>`, always passing the absolute build directory (a relative path silently builds the wrong tree). Run the test binary by absolute path. Fix every warning your new code introduces. This build takes a while; let it run.

5. Commit with a message written for someone who did not see this session: what the theme now exposes, the single-load change, each font-role decision in HeaderControls, and exactly what was built and run.

Report back: commit SHA and branch, the final ShellTheme.hpp public API (paste it), the role decisions, the test output, build warnings if any, and anything you could not do. You cannot run the app; say so rather than claiming a visual check.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
